hints: Focus on what making ethanoate ions really means, it means removing the acidic proton from ethanoic acid as in an acid-base reaction.
Notice that aqueous sodium carbonate is a base that will neutralise the acid to form the salt sodium ethanoate in solution.
Consider what happens when a weak acid dissolves in water versus when it is reduced by LiAlH4, only one of these leaves the ethanoate ion in solution.
walkthrough:
**Define the goal: make CH3COO-**

Pure ethanoic acid is mostly covalent molecules, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. To get ethanoate ions, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, we need an acid-base reaction that removes $\text{H}^+$ and leaves the anion in aqueous solution.

**Test reagent 1: aqueous sodium carbonate**

Carbonates neutralise acids to give salt + water + carbon dioxide. This gives soluble sodium ethanoate, so ethanoate ions are present.

Chemical equation:
$$2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + 2\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$

**Test reagent 2: LiAlH4**

$\text{LiAlH}_4$ is a powerful reducing agent, not a base for making a salt solution. It reduces the carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol.

Reaction type:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$
No ethanoate ions remain, the product is ethanol. So 2 is out.

**Test reagent 3: water**

Pure ethanoic acid in water acts as a weak acid and partially dissociates. Even though the equilibrium lies far left, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions are formed in solution.

Equilibrium:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$$
So 1 and 3 both work.

options.A: Incorrect because although 1 is correct, 2 is not. LiAlH4 reduces ethanoic acid to ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$), it does not produce a solution of ethanoate ions.
options.B: Correct because both 1 and 3 give ethanoate ions. Sodium carbonate neutralises the acid to sodium ethanoate solution, and water allows partial dissociation of the weak acid to $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$.
options.C: Incorrect because it misses reagent 3. Students often forget that simply dissolving a weak acid in water produces some of its conjugate base ions by partial dissociation.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes 2 and misses 1. LiAlH4 gives reduction to an alcohol, not an ionic salt solution, while the obvious acid-carbonate neutralisation in 1 is left out.
